A lower fuel-consumption rating can still produce a higher annual fuel bill

Translate L/100 km into annual litres and cash, compare different fuel prices, and chart how a city/highway distance mix can reverse the result.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Translate city/highway consumption into annual fuel cash at each vehicle’s entered price

Interactive planning lab

Vehicle A annual fuel-only cash$2,788
Vehicle B annual fuel-only cash$2,817.75
A minus B annual fuel cost; positive means B costs less-$29.75

Original hypothetical fuel-only comparison, not actual vehicle ratings, fuel quotes or a prediction of annual driving. Each vehicle travels the same entered annual kilometres and city-distance share. Litres per 100 km are weighted by distance, then multiplied by kilometres/100 and that vehicle’s required fuel price. The selected weighted consumption is 8.200 L/100 km for A and 7.225 for B. The entered annual fuel costs tie at 56.91% city-distance share. Fuel prices are constant over the modeled year. No purchase price, financing, depreciation, maintenance, insurance, tax calculation, non-fuel energy, equipment spending, time savings or resale value is included. The city/highway inputs may describe synthetic cases that do not match any actual vehicle; the tool does not recommend substituting a fuel type or grade. Laboratory labels are comparison tools, and actual consumption can differ with conditions. Display rounding does not feed back into the calculations.

The central idea

Compare fuel cash using the same driving distance, a supported consumption estimate and the price of the fuel each vehicle requires. A lower litres-per-100-kilometre figure answers only part of that question.

01

Read the units before copying a label into the budget

A vehicle’s fuel-consumption rating describes fuel used over a distance. A household fuel budget also needs the number of kilometres driven and the price paid for the fuel. Comparing one rating without those other inputs can produce the wrong cash conclusion.

Natural Resources Canada’s EnerGuide explanation says the combined consumption rating reflects 55% city and 45% highway driving. Its annual fuel-cost illustration uses the combined rating, 20,000 km and the stated fuel price. Those conventions help readers compare labels; they are not a measurement of any particular household’s driving.

The editable examples here use invented vehicles and fuel prices. Vehicle A is assigned 10 L/100 km in city conditions, 6 on the highway and CAD 1.70 per litre. B is assigned 7 in the city, 7.5 on the highway and CAD 1.95 per litre. These are neither real manufacturer ratings nor current pump prices. The contrasting patterns are chosen to make the arithmetic visible.

02

Weight the consumption by kilometres, not by time spent driving

The default annual distance is 20,000 km, with 55% in city conditions. That means 11,000 city kilometres and 9,000 highway kilometres. The relevant weight is distance because the consumption units are litres per 100 kilometres. Spending 55% of driving time in traffic would not, by itself, establish the same distance split.

For A, the selected weighted consumption is 10 × 0.55 + 6 × 0.45 = 8.2 L/100 km. For B it is 7 × 0.55 + 7.5 × 0.45 = 7.225 L/100 km. The first chart separates the city, highway and selected-mix comparisons. Its labels round consumption to one decimal, while the cash calculation retains full precision.

Do not use the simple average of city and highway figures unless the distance split is actually 50/50. Likewise, this illustrative weighted average does not attempt to reconstruct an official combined rating from rounded published inputs. Use the supported ratings and appropriate use assumptions for an actual comparison.

03

Convert the weighted rate into annual litres, then annual cash

The conversion is annual litres = annual kilometres ÷ 100 × weighted L/100 km. The units matter: multiplying the rate directly by 20,000 without dividing by 100 would overstate fuel use a hundredfold.

A therefore uses 20,000 ÷ 100 × 8.2 = 1,640 litres. B uses 20,000 ÷ 100 × 7.225 = 1,445 litres. B consumes 195 fewer litres over the same assumed distance, about 11.89% less than A.

Applying each entered price gives A an annual fuel budget of CAD 2,788 and B CAD 2,817.75. Although B uses less fuel, its fuel cash is CAD 29.75 higher. The difference comes from paying CAD 1.95 rather than CAD 1.70 for every litre B uses.

The second chart splits each total into fuel for city and highway kilometres. These segments are costs for distinct portions of the same year, so they can be added. Litres and dollars are not stacked together. The headline signed difference is A minus B: a positive result means B costs less, and the default negative CAD 29.75 means A costs less in fuel alone.

04

A consumption crossover and a cash crossover need not coincide

The synthetic vehicles have different strengths across the two conditions. A uses less fuel per kilometre on the highway, while B uses less in the city. Their distance-weighted consumption rates are equal at a city share of one-third: 6 + 4w = 7.5 − 0.5w, where w is the city-distance fraction.

Fuel cash uses a different equality because each rate is multiplied by its own price. A costs CAD 10.20 + CAD 6.80w per 100 km; B costs CAD 14.625 − CAD 0.975w per 100 km. These are equal at w = 4.425 ÷ 7.775, or about 56.91% city distance.

Between those two shares, B uses fewer litres but A still has lower fuel cash. The signed line chart focuses on this cash comparison and its zero crossing. The equality describes the entered prices and consumption patterns; it does not set a universal city-driving threshold for any kind of vehicle.

If both cost patterns are identical, every mix ties. Other inputs may have no equality anywhere between entirely highway and entirely city driving. The model states those cases explicitly. At zero annual distance, both fuel budgets are zero regardless of the mix.

05

Change the driving mix and fuel price separately

Raise city distance from 55% to 80%, holding total kilometres and both prices fixed. A’s weighted use becomes 9.2 L/100 km and B’s 7.1. Their annual fuel costs become CAD 3,128 and CAD 2,769, so B now costs CAD 359 less in fuel.

Alternatively, keep the default 55% city split but change B’s hypothetical fuel price to CAD 1.70. B’s fuel budget becomes CAD 2,456.50, CAD 331.50 below A. That test isolates price; the prior test isolated use. Neither establishes that a different fuel grade is suitable for a real vehicle.

The matrix varies both city-distance share and B’s fuel price. Its fixed cases are a comparison aid rather than a forecast of local prices. Doubling annual kilometres doubles all modeled fuel cash and differences, but it does not move a unique city-share crossover when prices and consumption remain fixed.

06

Replace the illustration with evidence from the actual vehicle and route

Natural Resources Canada explains that standardized test ratings do not capture every road condition. Driving behaviour, weather, traffic, vehicle condition and powered accessories can affect actual consumption. The tool does not estimate those effects or add a universal adjustment percentage.

For a household plan, record supported fuel requirements, relevant ratings or measured consumption, expected distance and a dated price assumption. A route change may alter both total kilometres and the city/highway mix. Test those effects explicitly instead of changing only a single combined rating.

This page compares fuel spending. Purchase prices, loan interest, depreciation, maintenance, insurance, parking and eventual resale belong in a broader vehicle budget. A favourable fuel result alone does not establish a lower total ownership cost or justify a purchase premium. The related ownership and repair guides address those different cash decisions.
